prompt.context: The client is a company that installs and maintains traffic signals. It is a small company based in California. They are considering expanding into the Tri-state market, especially Manhattan. They want our help to determine whether they should enter the Manhattan market.
prompt.question: Should the client enter the Manhattan traffic signal market?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's goal for entering this market?
clarifying_info.a: Increase revenues and profits. There is no specific ROI target.

clarifying_info.q: Is the scope of this case limited to the Manhattan market?
Does the client manufacture traffic signals?
clarifying_info.a: No. They only install and maintain signals.

exhibits.title: Market Size of Traffic Signals in Manhattan
exhibits.shows: A structured breakdown of the market sizing approach for Manhattan traffic signals, including information provided up front and data to be provided if asked.
exhibits.data: Price of one signal system (install): $100,000; Maintenance per signal per year: $15,000; Each system lasts 20 years; Approximate shape of Manhattan: 80 streets long x 25 streets wide

exhibits.title: NPV of Project
exhibits.shows: A cost breakdown for installation and maintenance labor, along with revenue and cost figures for a 3-year contract period used to calculate project NPV.
exhibits.data: Contract duration: 3 years; Installation labor: 5 workers, $35/hr, 6 hrs per signal system; Maintenance labor: 2 workers, 4 hrs per signal system, 2 incidents per year; Cost of signal system: $85,000; Transportation cost: $0 (sourced locally)

framework: Market sizing: Estimate number of intersections in Manhattan and derive installation and maintenance market size
Competitive landscape: Identify the incumbent and assess competitive dynamics
Business model: Understand contract structure (single contract covering all signals, awarded by bid)
Financial analysis: Calculate revenues, costs, and NPV over the contract period
Recommendation: Assess profitability and strategic importance; determine bid price

questions.prompt: Size the Manhattan traffic signal market — estimate the installation market and the maintenance market.
questions.guidance: The candidate should estimate intersections by modeling Manhattan's grid shape, then apply replacement rate and pricing to get installation market, and full-stock pricing for maintenance market.

math.setup: Model Manhattan as approximately 80 streets long x 25 streets wide (tapered shape). Intersections = 80 x 25 = 2,000. Installation market: 1/20 of signals replaced each year (20-year lifespan). Revenue per install = $100,000. Maintenance market: all 2,000 signals maintained each year at $15,000/signal.

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of the project over the 3-year contract.
questions.guidance: The candidate should calculate revenues and costs for Year 1 (install + maintenance) and Years 2–3 (maintenance only), then derive NPV. A simplified approach (no discounting, or light discounting) is acceptable given the level of precision.

math.setup: Year 1 revenues = $10M (installation) + $30M (maintenance) = $40M. Years 2 and 3 revenues = $30M/year (maintenance only). Cost of signal system = $85,000. Installation labor = 5 workers x $35/hr x 6 hrs = $1,050 per system. Total install cost per system = $85,000 + $1,050 = $86,050. Maintenance labor = 2 workers x $35/hr x 4 hrs x 2 incidents = $560 per signal per year. Year 1 install costs = 100 signals x $86,050 = $8.605M ≈ $8.6M. Year 1 maintenance costs = 2,000 x $560 = $1.12M. Year 2 and 3 maintenance costs = $1.12M x 2 = $2.24M each year.
steps: Year 2 revenue = $30M; Year 2 costs = $2.24M; Year 2 profit = $27.76M
Year 3 revenue = $30M; Year 3 costs = $2.24M; Year 3 profit = $27.76M

brainstorming.prompt: Why might the client want to bid at a loss on this contract?

categories.name: Strategic positioning
ideas: Manhattan is the largest traffic signal market in the US — winning it establishes credibility
A Manhattan win signals capability to handle large-scale city contracts
Could open doors to other major Northeast and national city contracts

categories.name: Market entry and scale
ideas: Establishes a foothold in the Tri-state market
Builds relationships with municipal buyers and regulators
Creates a reference contract to win future bids elsewhere

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Displacing the incumbent (largest Northeast player) weakens a key competitor
Prevents competitor from reinforcing dominance in Manhattan

recommendation: Yes, the client should enter the Manhattan market and bid for the contract
The project generates an NPV of approximately $88M, making it financially attractive
Manhattan is the largest traffic signal market in the US and winning it carries significant strategic value — it can unlock contracts in other major cities
risks: Implementation risk: the client has not previously managed a contract of this scale or in a large city environment
Risk of underestimating costs or operational complexity in a dense urban setting
Incumbent competitor has an established presence in the Northeast and may bid aggressively
next_steps: Investigate historical bids submitted by competitors on previous Manhattan-area contracts
Quantify the strategic value of the Manhattan contract (potential downstream revenue from other cities) to determine the maximum rational bid
Assess operational readiness: staffing, logistics, and local sourcing capacity for a large-scale installation
